text: A read-through cache sits between the application and the database. On a miss the cache loads the value from the backing store, saves it, and returns it, so callers never talk to the database directly. The pattern keeps cache population logic in one place, but a cold cache still sends every first read downstream, and a popular key expiring can send a burst of identical loads at once.

Cache invalidation is the hard half of caching. Time-based expiry is simple but serves stale values for the whole window, while explicit invalidation on write is precise but couples every writer to the cache topology. Most teams land on short TTLs plus best-effort invalidation, accepting a bounded staleness window in exchange for not having to enumerate every code path that mutates the underlying row.

The thundering herd problem shows up when a hot cache entry expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss at the same moment. Every one of them independently queries the database and tries to repopulate the same key. Request coalescing fixes this by letting the first miss take a lock and do the load while the rest wait for that single result instead of stampeding the backing store.

A B-tree index keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree whose nodes match the page size of the disk. Lookups, range scans, and ordered iteration all become logarithmic in the number of rows. The price is paid on writes: every insert or update must also update each index that covers the changed columns, which is why tables with many indexes ingest data noticeably slower.

A composite index on two columns is only fully useful when queries filter on its leading column. The index stores entries sorted by the first column, then the second, so a query that filters only on the second column cannot seek and falls back to scanning. Column order in the index definition is therefore a real design decision, not a cosmetic one.

Query planners choose between an index seek and a full table scan using cost estimates built from table statistics. When statistics go stale after a bulk load, the planner can badly misjudge row counts and pick a nested loop join over millions of rows. Refreshing statistics is often the actual fix for a query that suddenly became slow without any code change.

A token bucket limiter refills at a fixed rate up to a burst capacity. Each request takes one token and is rejected or delayed when the bucket is empty. The refill rate sets the sustained throughput while the bucket depth sets how large a burst can pass unthrottled, and tuning those two numbers independently is the main advantage over a plain fixed-window counter.

Fixed-window rate limiting counts requests per clock window and resets the counter at the boundary. Its known weakness is the boundary burst: a client can spend a full quota in the last second of one window and another full quota in the first second of the next, doubling the intended rate. Sliding-window counters smooth this by weighting the previous window into the current estimate.

When a service rejects a request with a retry hint, well-behaved clients back off exponentially and add jitter so their retries do not synchronize. Without jitter, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment too, and the recovered service is immediately knocked over again by the coordinated wave. Randomizing the delay spreads that load across the whole interval.

A container scheduler places pods onto nodes by filtering out machines that fail hard constraints and then scoring the rest. Resource requests, not live usage, drive the placement math, so a cluster can look full to the scheduler while its nodes sit mostly idle. Getting requests close to real consumption is the single highest-leverage tuning knob in most deployments.

Liveness and readiness probes answer different questions. A failing liveness probe tells the orchestrator to restart the container because it is wedged. A failing readiness probe only removes the pod from the load balancer until it recovers. Wiring a slow dependency check into the liveness probe is a classic mistake that turns a brief downstream blip into a rolling restart storm.

Rolling deployments replace instances a few at a time, watching health checks between batches, so capacity never drops below a configured floor. The rollback story is what makes the strategy valuable: when the new version starts failing its checks, the rollout pauses automatically and the old replica set is still there to scale back up. Blue-green trades double the hardware for an even faster switch.

A unit test earns its keep by failing when the behavior it pins changes. Tests that assert on incidental details like private call order or exact log strings break on harmless refactors and train the team to update tests mechanically. Asserting on observable behavior through the public interface keeps the suite meaningful and makes a red build worth investigating.

Test doubles come in grades. A stub returns canned values, a fake carries a working lightweight implementation like an in-memory repository, and a mock records calls for later verification. Overusing mocks couples tests to implementation structure, because the test now encodes which collaborators were called in which order rather than what the code actually produced for the caller.

Flaky tests are usually a hidden dependency on time, ordering, or shared state. A test that sleeps and polls a real clock will pass locally and fail under CI load, while injecting a controllable clock makes the same scenario deterministic. Quarantining flaky tests without fixing the root cause just moves the uncertainty into production, where the same race still exists.

At-least-once delivery means the queue redelivers a message whenever it cannot prove the consumer finished, so every consumer must be idempotent. Deduplication keys, upserts, and conditional writes turn a redelivered message into a harmless no-op. Exactly-once processing is really at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent handling, because the network can always fail after the work but before the acknowledgment.

A dead letter queue catches messages that keep failing after a bounded number of delivery attempts. Without one, a single malformed message can block a partition forever while the consumer crashes, restarts, and receives the same poison payload again. Parking the message aside keeps the stream flowing and preserves the evidence for a human to inspect later.

Consumer lag is the distance between the newest message in the log and the position a consumer group has committed. Rising lag under steady input means the consumers cannot keep up, and the usual levers are batching, more partitions, or cheaper per-message work. Lag that grows only during traffic spikes and drains afterward is capacity planning working exactly as intended.

A TLS handshake establishes three things before any application byte moves: that the server is who it claims, which cipher both sides support, and a shared symmetric key. Certificate verification walks the chain from the server certificate to a trusted root, checking signatures and validity windows. Only after the handshake completes does the connection switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual payload.

Certificate expiry is a fully predictable outage that still takes production systems down every week somewhere. The fix is boring automation: short-lived certificates renewed automatically well before their deadline, monitoring on days remaining, and an alert threshold long enough to fix a broken renewal pipeline. Manual renewal calendars fail exactly once, on the weekend the owner is on vacation.

Session resumption lets a client skip the expensive part of a repeat TLS handshake by presenting a ticket from a previous connection. This saves a round trip and significant CPU on both ends, which matters at scale for short-lived connections. The tradeoff is that ticket keys become long-lived secrets, and rotating them too slowly weakens forward secrecy across everything they protected.

Generational collectors bet that most objects die young. New allocations land in a small nursery that is collected often and cheaply, while survivors get promoted to an old generation that is collected rarely. The bet pays off for typical request-response workloads, but a cache that holds objects just long enough to be promoted defeats the heuristic and inflates old-generation pressure.

A stop-the-world pause halts every application thread while the collector scans the heap. Concurrent collectors shrink these pauses by doing most marking while the application runs, paying instead with write barriers and some throughput. Which side of that trade you want depends on the workload: a batch job cares about total throughput, a trading gateway cares about the worst pause.

Reference counting frees objects the moment their last reference drops, giving prompt reclamation and no global pauses. Its blind spot is cycles: two objects pointing at each other never reach a count of zero even when nothing else can see them. Systems built on reference counting either add a cycle detector that runs periodically or ask programmers to break cycles with weak references.
